newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji PM Rabuka defends coup 10 years on.
newsitem.headline: Fiji PM Rabuka defends coup 10 years on.

text.p: Fiji Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka on Wednesday defended the racially-motivated coup which brought him to power, but called on Fiji to mark the 10th anniversary of the bloodless military coup with national unity.

"Ten years ago today...I was convinced there was no other way to safeguard the national security interests of Fiji," Rabuka said in an emotional speech to parliament as he tabled a report on Fiji's racially-biased constitution.

"Today I can say with the same strength of conviction that I believe there is only one way. We must stand together. A house divided against itself cannot stand," said Rabuka, who was Fiji's military commander at the time of the coup in 1987.
"Whether we like it or not we have been brought together by history and circumstances," he said.
On May 14, 1987, Rabuka led a group of balaclava-wearing troops into the Fijian parliament and kidnapped the then Indian-dominated government led by Timoci Bavadra.
Rabuka said he staged the coup because he felt indigenous Fijians were losing control of their country to Indians, who dominate the South Pacific nation's economy.
Rabuka introduced a racially-biased constitution which guaranteed indigenous Fijians a majority in the country's 70-seat parliament and went on to be elected prime minister.
Fiji was thrown out of the British Commonwealth as a result of the coup and has been stopped from rejoining because of Indian government opposition.
But while suspicions still exist between Indian and indigenous Fijians, political leaders have begun to co-operate as Rabuka moves towards a more balanced constitution.
A Rabuka-backed constitutional review conducted last year called for 45 non-ethnic seats, 12 indigenous Fijian seats, 10 ethnic Indian seats and a handful of other minor ethnic seats.
Jai Ram Reddy, head of the Indian-based opposition National Federation Party, on Wednesday backed Rabuka's call for unity and described the former army colonel as a decisive leader.

"I think he is providing very good, firm, decisive leadership in this critical stage in our history to repair some of the wounds of the military coup...and put the country back on a more even keel, a more multi-racial track," Reddy said.
Indian Fijians make up about 46 percent of Fiji's 750,000 population. Indians were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on the country's sugar cane plantations.
